# Configuration reference (`openshell.json`, version 1)

OpenShell looks for `openshell.json` or `openshell.toml` in the given directory and its parents. All relative paths
are resolved against the directory containing the file. Unknown fields are errors (typos are caught early).
Editor completion: add `"$schema": "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RobinsSuperSchmiede/EDA/main/schema/openshell.schema.json"`.
`openshell schema` prints the schema; `openshell doctor` validates the file and the environment.

## Top level

| Field | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `version` | number | Schema version, currently `1` (default). Newer versions are rejected with a clear message. |
| `app` | object | `name` (required), `id`, `version` (semver, needed for installers), `description`, `icon` (PNG for window and installers). |
| `window` | object | Native window settings. |
| `frontend` | object | What the window shows. |
| `services` | array | Backends, databases, workers, AI servers, … |
| `databases` | array | Built-in SQLite databases managed by OpenShell. |
| `runtime` | object | Runtime manager behaviour. |
| `agents` | object | Agent Interaction Layer: on/off (opt-in), permissions, approvals, providers. |
| `capabilities` | array | Functions the app exposes to agents (HTTP endpoint, script, task). |
| `tasks` | object | Named commands (`"test": "pytest"`), runnable by agents with the `system` scope. |
| `package` | object | Installer settings – see [installers.md](installers.md). |
| `runtimes` | object | Language runtimes shipped inside the app – see [`runtimes`](#runtimes). |

## `window`

| Field | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `title` | `app.name` | Window title |
| `width`, `height` | 1280, 800 | Initial size |
| `min_width`, `min_height` | – | Minimum size (both required to take effect) |
| `resizable` | `true` | |
| `maximized` | `false` | |
| `close_to_tray` | `false` | Closing hides the window; services keep running |
| `title_bar` | `"native"` | `"overlay"`: the frontend draws the title bar (see [sdk.md](sdk.md#own-title-bar)). No system title bar on Windows/Linux; window buttons over the content on macOS |
| `tray` | `true` | Show a tray icon (show, reload, runtime panel, restart services, quit) |
| `devtools` | dev mode only | Allow WebView devtools |
| `enabled` | `true` | `false`: no window – the app runs in the tray / background (services, databases, agent functions). Apps without a frontend show OpenShell's console in the window |

## `frontend`

OpenShell does not care which framework you use. It needs one of:

- `command` + `url` (or `port`): a process that serves the frontend (dev server, local web server),
- `url` alone: an already running or remote frontend,
- `dist`: a directory of built files that OpenShell serves itself.

| Field | Description |
|---|---|
| `command` | Shell string (`"npm run dev"`) or argv array |
| `cwd` | Working directory |
| `env` | Extra environment variables (values support `${...}`) |
| `port` | Number or `"auto"`; available as `${port}` and `$PORT` |
| `url` | URL loaded into the window |
| `dist` | Built frontend directory (production) |
| `build` | Build command for `openshell build` |
| `setup` | One-time step, e.g. `{ "command": "npm install", "creates": "frontend/node_modules" }` |
| `proxy` | Static server reverse proxy, e.g. `{ "/api": "${services.backend.url}" }` |
| `watch` | Paths that reload the window when changed (dev mode; useful for static frontends) |
| `healthcheck` | Override readiness check (default: the URL answers) |
| `depends_on` | Services that must be healthy first |
| `production` | Overrides for production mode: `{ "command", "url", "dist" }` |

Mode selection: **development** uses `command`/`url`, falling back to `dist`. **Production** uses `production`
overrides, then `dist`, then the development settings.

## `services[]`

| Field | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | – | Unique, `[a-z0-9_-]` (`frontend` is reserved) |
| `description`, `kind` | – | Informational (`backend`, `database`, `worker`, `ai`, …) |
| `command` | – | Shell string or argv. In argv form `python` falls back to `python3` (and vice versa) |
| `args` | `[]` | Appended arguments |
| `cwd` | project root | |
| `env` | `{}` | Values support `${...}` |
| `port` | – | Number or `"auto"`; exported as `PORT` |
| `url` | `http://127.0.0.1:<port>` | Base URL (used by `${services.<name>.url}` and HTTP capabilities) |
| `external` | `false` | Do not start; only monitor (`url` / `healthcheck` required) |
| `healthcheck` | TCP on `port` | URL string (HTTP 2xx/3xx) or `{ "http" \| "tcp", "interval_ms", "timeout_ms", "failure_threshold", "ready_timeout_ms" }` |
| `restart` | `true` (on-failure) | `true`, `false`, `"never"`, `"on-failure"`, `"always"` |
| `max_restarts` | 5 | Crashes per minute before the service is marked `failed` |
| `depends_on` | `[]` | Started after these are healthy; stopped before them |
| `autostart` | `true` | Start with the runtime |
| `setup` | – | One-time step (`command`, `creates`, `cwd`) |
| `build` | – | Build step for compiled services: command, or `{ "command", "cwd", "on_start": "development" \| "always" \| "never" }`. Runs before every start in dev mode and in `openshell build` / `package`. See [languages.md](languages.md) |
| `openapi` | – | Import the service's OpenAPI 3 (JSON) document as agent tools: `"/openapi.json"`, URL, project file, or `{ "location", "include", "exclude", "prefix" }` |
| `watch` | `[]` | Paths whose changes restart the service (dev mode). `node_modules`, `.git`, `__pycache__`, `target`, `.venv`, `*.log` are ignored |
| `modes` | all | Only run in `["development"]` or `["production"]` |
| `platforms` | all | Only run on `desktop`, `android` and/or `server`, e.g. `["desktop", "server"]` for a service that needs a toolchain. See [platforms.md](platforms.md) |
| `background` | `keep` | Mobile platforms: `pause` stops the service while the app is in the background and starts it again afterwards |
| `stop_timeout_ms` | `runtime.shutdown_timeout_ms` | Grace period before a forced kill (Unix; Windows terminates the tree immediately) |
| `requires` | `{}` | Runtime versions the service needs, e.g. `{ "python": ">=3.10", "java": ">=17" }`. Known runtimes: `python`, `node`, `java`, `dotnet`, `go`, `rust`. Checked by `openshell doctor` (error) and when the app starts (warning in the service's log). The frontend has the same field for its dev server (`"requires": { "node": ">=18" }`) |

Version requirements: `>=3.10`, `>3`, `<=21`, `<4`, `=3.12.1`, `3.12` (same as `=3.12`, matches 3.12.x),
`^1.2` (`>=1.2 <2`), `~1.2` (`>=1.2 <1.3`), combined with commas: `">=3.10, <3.13"`.

Every process also receives `OPENSHELL=1`, `OPENSHELL_MODE`, `OPENSHELL_SERVICE`, `OPENSHELL_PROJECT_ROOT`,
`OPENSHELL_CONTROL_URL`, `OPENSHELL_DATA_DIR` (writable per-app data directory – per user for installed apps; store
databases and files there) and `PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1` (unless set).

## Variables

Usable in commands, args, env values, URLs, health checks and proxy targets:

| Variable | Value |
|---|---|
| `${port}` | Port of the current service / frontend |
| `${services.<name>.port}` / `${services.<name>.url}` | Another service |
| `${frontend.url}` | Frontend URL |
| `${project.root}` | Absolute project directory |
| `${mode}` | `development` / `production` |
| `${env.NAME}` | Environment variable of the shell |
| `$$` | Literal `$` |

## `runtime`

| Field | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `autostart` | `true` | Start services when the shell starts |
| `background_mode` | `false` | Keep running in the tray when the window is closed |
| `control_port` | random | Fixed port for the control API |
| `log_buffer_lines` | 10000 | Lines kept in memory (files in `.openshell/logs/`) |
| `shutdown_timeout_ms` | 5000 | Default grace period when stopping |
| `launch_at_login` | `false` | Start the installed app when the user logs in (installed apps only) |
| `remote` | off | Remote access for other devices – see [`runtime.remote`](#runtimeremote) |

### `runtime.remote`

Makes the app usable from other devices (a laptop using an app hosted on a phone, an agent on another machine).
Everything except `enabled` is optional. Full guide: [remote-access.md](remote-access.md).

| Field | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `enabled` | `false` | Start the gateway (app profile over MCP) and the exposed ports |
| `bind` | `0.0.0.0` | Address to listen on; a VPN address (Tailscale `100.x.y.z`) limits access to your devices |
| `port` | 7420 | Gateway port |
| `allow` | everyone | IP addresses / CIDR ranges that may connect, e.g. `["192.168.1.0/24", "100.64.0.0/10"]`. Loopback is always allowed |
| `shared_token` | `true` | Accept the shared pairing token; `false` = only per-device tokens (`openshell remote pair <device>`) |
| `rate_limit` | 120 / 10 / 5 | `{ "requests_per_minute": 120, "max_failed_auth": 10, "block_minutes": 5 }` per address; `0` switches a limit off |
| `tls` | off | `{ "enabled": true }` with a self-signed certificate (clients pin its SHA-256 fingerprint), or `{ "enabled": true, "cert": "certs/fullchain.pem", "key": "certs/key.pem" }` |
| `expose` | none | Services reachable on their own port: `[{ "service": "api", "port": 8080 }]` – see below |

`expose[]` entries:

| Field | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `service` | – | Service name, or `frontend` |
| `port` | – | Port other devices connect to (must differ from the gateway and control ports) |
| `protocol` | `http` | `http` (websites, APIs; token login, TLS) or `tcp` (any protocol, e.g. PostgreSQL, Redis, MQTT) |
| `auth` | `token` for `http` | `token`: pairing/device token as `Authorization: Bearer`, cookie, or once `?openshell_token=…` in the browser; `none`: no login (use `allow`). `tcp` is always `none` |
| `allow` | `runtime.remote.allow` | Addresses / CIDR ranges for this port only |

## `agents`

| Field | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `enabled` | `false` | **Opt-in.** `true` opens the agent layer: MCP endpoints (`/mcp`, `/mcp/app`, `--mcp`), the tools API, the UI bridge and the remote gateway's MCP endpoint. While `false` they refuse every request and the UI bridge is not injected; the app, its frontend SDK and exposed services keep working. `openshell create`, `openshell init` and `openshell add function` write `true`; `openshell agents enable` / `disable` switch it |
| `permissions` | dev: `read, ui, actions, services, files, code` · prod: `read, ui, actions` | A list for all modes or `{ "development": [...], "production": [...] }` |
| `approval_required` | `["system"]` | Scopes that need a human decision |
| `approval_timeout_ms` | 120000 | Unanswered requests are denied |
| `sdk_permissions` | `["read", "ui"]` | Scopes for the frontend SDK (app token) |
| `providers` | `[]` | `{ "name", "kind": "ollama" \| "lm-studio" \| "openai-compatible" \| "openai" \| "anthropic" \| "mcp" \| "custom", "url", "api_key_env", "models" }` |
| `detect_local_providers` | `true` | Probe Ollama (11434) and LM Studio (1234) |

Permission scopes: `read`, `ui`, `actions` (alias `write`), `services`, `files`, `code`, `system`.

Agent sessions (`openshell agents token <name> --scopes read,actions`) and paired devices
(`openshell remote pair <device> --scopes read`) get their own tokens and scopes; they never get more than
`permissions` grants in the current mode. See [agents.md](agents.md#agent-sessions).

## `runtimes`

Language runtimes shipped inside the app, so the user's machine needs no Python, Node.js or Java:

```json
"runtimes": {
  "python": "3.12",
  "node": { "version": "22", "path": "vendor/node" },
  "java": "21"
}
```

| Runtime | Downloaded from | Default version |
|---|---|---|
| `python` | python-build-standalone (`install_only` builds) | `3.12` |
| `node` | nodejs.org | `22` |
| `java` | Eclipse Temurin JRE (adoptium.net) | `21` |

A value is a version (`"22"`, `"3.12"`, `"21.0.5"`) or `{ "version", "path" }` (default path `runtimes/<name>`,
inside the project). `openshell runtime install` downloads every declared runtime for the current system and checks
its SHA-256; `openshell runtime add <name> [version]` declares and downloads in one step. The runtime's executable
folders are put in front of `PATH` for every service, setup and build step, function and task, so `python main.py`
or `npm install` use the bundled copy. `openshell package` ships the folder with the app. A runtime is built for one
operating system: build installers on each system (the release workflow runs `openshell runtime install` there).
Downloaded runtimes do not belong in git; `runtime add` adds the folder to `.gitignore`.

## `capabilities[]`

```json
{
  "name": "add_todo",
  "description": "Create a todo",
  "permission": "actions",
  "input_schema": { "type": "object", "properties": { "title": { "type": "string" } }, "required": ["title"] },
  "http": { "service": "backend", "method": "POST", "path": "/api/todos" }
}
```

Exactly one target:

- `http` – `service` + `path`, or `url`; GET/DELETE send the input as query parameters, other methods as JSON body.
- `run` – a script/program: `["python", "tools/x.py"]` or `{ "command", "cwd", "env", "timeout_ms" }`. It receives the
  input as JSON on stdin (and in `OPENSHELL_INPUT`) and prints its result (JSON or text) on stdout; a non-zero exit
  code is an error (message from stderr). No server needed – see [building-blocks.md](building-blocks.md#functions).
- `task` – name of a task (input is ignored).

Agents see each capability as a tool `cap_<name>` (developer profile), under its plain name (app profile) and via
`app_invoke`. The frontend calls them with `OpenShell.invoke(name, input)`.

## `databases[]`

```json
{ "name": "main", "migrations": "db/migrations", "agent_access": "write" }
```

| Field | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | – | `[a-z0-9_]`; services get the path as `OPENSHELL_DB_<NAME>` |
| `type` | `"sqlite"` | Engine (SQLite is built in) |
| `path` | `<name>.db` | File, relative to the app's data directory (`OPENSHELL_DATA_DIR`) or absolute |
| `migrations` | – | Folder of `*.sql` files, applied once each in file-name order |
| `agent_access` | `"read"` | `none`, `read` (`db_list`, `db_schema`, `db_query`) or `write` (also `db_execute`) |
| `description` | – | Shown to agents |

The main (or only) database is also exported as `DATABASE_URL=sqlite:///…`. Details:
[building-blocks.md](building-blocks.md#database).

## TOML

```toml
version = 1

[app]
name = "My App"

[frontend]
command = "npm run dev"
cwd = "frontend"
url = "http://localhost:5173"

[[services]]
name = "api"
command = ["node", "server.js"]
port = 3001
restart = "always"
```


================================================================================
FILE: docs/languages.md
================================================================================

# Languages: C++, Java and others

OpenShell runs any executable, so every language works. Compiled languages use a **`build`** step:

- in **development** mode the build runs before every start – and therefore after every file change in `watch`,
  so editing `src/` recompiles and restarts the service automatically,
- `openshell build` / `openshell package` run all builds for production,
- a failing build marks the service `failed` with the compiler output in the logs (also readable by agents via
  `logs_read {"errors_only": true}`); fixing the code retries automatically.

```json
"build": "cmake --build build"                                       // shell string
"build": ["javac", "-d", "build/classes", "src/Main.java"]           // argv
"build": { "command": "mvn -q package", "cwd": "backend", "on_start": "never" }   // development (default) | always | never
```

Templates: `openshell create my-app -t vanilla-java` and `-t vanilla-cpp`. `openshell init` detects Maven, Gradle,
Spring Boot, plain `javac` sources, CMake and Makefiles.

## Support levels

`openshell languages` prints this table from the same data the CLI uses:

| Language | Level | Runtime on the target machine | Templates |
|---|---|---|---|
| Python | tested | Python, or bundled (`openshell runtime add python`) | `vanilla-python`, `react-python`, `vue-python` |
| Node.js | tested | Node.js, or bundled (`openshell runtime add node`) | `react-node` |
| Java / Spring Boot | tested | a JRE, or bundled (`openshell runtime add java`) | `vanilla-java` |
| C++ (CMake) | tested | none (compiled) | `vanilla-cpp` |
| Go | less tested | none (`go build`) | `svelte-go` |
| Rust | less tested | none (`cargo build`) | – |
| .NET | less tested | .NET runtime, or none when published self-contained | – |
| anything else | by contract | whatever it needs | – |

*Tested* means CI creates the template, runs it headless on Windows, macOS and Linux, waits until every service is
healthy, loads the frontend and calls an agent function (`scripts/e2e-templates.py`). *By contract*: any program
that reads `PORT`, binds `127.0.0.1` and answers `/health` works.

Each language is one unit in the code: an entry in `crates/config/src/runtimes.rs` (runtime, version probe, support
level, templates) and a detector in `crates/cli/src/languages/` for `openshell init`.

## Versions

Pin what a service needs with `requires` – `openshell doctor` reports a mismatch as an error, the app logs a warning
when it starts:

```json
{ "name": "api", "command": ["python", "main.py"], "requires": { "python": ">=3.10, <3.14" } }
```

Known runtimes: `python`, `node`, `java`, `dotnet`, `go`, `rust`. To not depend on the user's machine at all, bundle
the runtime (see [installers.md](installers.md#runtimes)).

## Java

### Plain JDK (template `vanilla-java`)

```json
{
  "name": "backend",
  "cwd": "backend",
  "build": ["javac", "-d", "build/classes", "src/Main.java"],
  "command": ["java", "-cp", "build/classes", "Main"],
  "port": "auto",
  "healthcheck": "http://127.0.0.1:${port}/health",
  "watch": ["backend/src"]
}
```

### Spring Boot

```json
{
  "name": "backend",
  "cwd": "backend",
  "command": ["mvnw", "-q", "spring-boot:run", "-Dspring-boot.run.arguments=--server.port=${port}"],
  "port": "auto",
  "healthcheck": { "http": "http://127.0.0.1:${port}/actuator/health", "ready_timeout_ms": 120000 },
  "openapi": "/v3/api-docs",
  "watch": ["backend/src"]
}
```

`mvnw` / `gradlew` are found in the service directory on all platforms. With
[springdoc-openapi](https://springdoc.org) the `openapi` field turns every REST endpoint into an agent tool.
For production use the jar:

```json
"build": { "command": ["mvnw", "-q", "-DskipTests", "package"], "on_start": "never" },
"command": ["java", "-jar", "target/app-1.0.0.jar", "--server.port=${port}"]
```

Gradle: `["gradlew", "-q", "bootRun", "--args=--server.port=${port}"]`.

Java UI apps (Swing/JavaFX) cannot be embedded into the WebView; run them as a service if they offer an HTTP API, or
use OpenShell for their web front end.

## C++

### CMake (template `vanilla-cpp`)

```json
{
  "name": "backend",
  "cwd": "backend",
  "build": "cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release && cmake --build build --config Release",
  "command": ["build/bin/todo-server"],
  "port": "auto",
  "watch": ["backend/src", "backend/CMakeLists.txt"]
}
```

- `command` paths without extension also find `name.exe` on Windows.
- Multi-config generators (Visual Studio) put binaries into `build/Release/` – the template sets
  `CMAKE_RUNTIME_OUTPUT_DIRECTORY` so the path is `build/bin` everywhere.
- On Windows run OpenShell from a *Developer PowerShell* (or install CMake + Ninja / MinGW) so the compiler is found.
- Ship only the binary: `"package": { "include": ["openshell.json", "web", "backend/build/bin"] }`.
- HTTP libraries such as cpp-httplib, Crow, Drogon or Boost.Beast work the same way.

## Others

| Language | `build` | `command` |
|---|---|---|
| Rust | `cargo build --release` | `["target/release/server"]` |
| Go | `go build -o bin/server .` | `["bin/server"]` (or `go run .` without build) |
| C# / .NET | `dotnet build -c Release` | `["dotnet", "run", "--no-build", "-c", "Release", "--", "--urls", "http://127.0.0.1:${port}"]` (`openshell init` detects `*.csproj`) |
| Kotlin (Ktor) | – | `["gradlew", "-q", "run"]` |
| Python | – (`setup` for `pip install`) | `["python", "main.py"]` |
| Node.js / Deno / Bun | – | `["node", "server.js"]`, `["deno", "run", "-A", "main.ts"]` |

ASP.NET (Swashbuckle), FastAPI, NestJS and Spring all publish OpenAPI documents – set `openapi` and agents can use
the backend without UI automation.


================================================================================
FILE: docs/agents.md
================================================================================

# Agent Interaction Layer

OpenShell gives AI agents a standardized, model-agnostic interface to a running desktop application – in two
profiles:

| Profile | For | Tools |
|---|---|---|
| **app** ("use the app") | assistants that should *work with* the application, e.g. Claude Desktop on the user's PC | only the application's own functions (`list_todos`, `add_todo`, …) + `app_status` |
| **full** ("develop the app") | coding agents that build and evolve the application | everything below: runtime, logs, services, files, UI automation, capabilities |

Neither profile needs the UI: the app profile calls the application's API directly; UI automation is an *extra*
for the full profile.

In the full profile agents can

- query application and runtime state, read logs,
- start, stop and restart services,
- see and operate the user interface (semantic snapshot, click, fill, navigate, …),
- discover and invoke application capabilities,
- read and modify project files (scoped to the project),
- run declared tasks,

all subject to permission scopes, optional human approval and an audit log. OpenShell does not ship or prescribe an
AI model – it is infrastructure for any agent: Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenAI- or Anthropic-based agents, local
models via Ollama / LM Studio, or your own agent system.

**The agent layer is opt-in.** An app opens it with `"agents": { "enabled": true }` – `openshell create`,
`openshell init` and `openshell add function` write that for you, `openshell agents enable` / `disable` switch it.
While it is off, the MCP endpoints, the tools API, the UI bridge and the remote gateway's MCP endpoint refuse every
request and no bridge script is injected into the app's pages; the app, its frontend SDK and exposed services keep
working. `openshell agents` shows what agents get right now.

## Connecting

### Using an installed app

Installed apps (see [installers.md](installers.md)) are MCP servers themselves:

```json
{ "mcpServers": { "my-app": { "command": "C:\\Users\\me\\AppData\\Local\\Programs\\My App\\my-app.exe", "args": ["--mcp"] } } }
```

If the app is not running, it starts **in the background without a window**, so an agent can use it while the user
does something else. Opening the app later replaces the background instance with the window. The tool list contains
only the app's functions; permissions follow `agents.permissions.production`. Add `--profile full` for the developer
tool set. The runtime panel (title bar right-click → *Runtime panel*) shows both commands ready to copy.

### Using a project from the CLI

```bash
openshell mcp --app --start --project /path/to/app   # app profile, start headless (production) if needed
```

### Developing: MCP over stdio (recommended)

```bash
openshell mcp --project /path/to/app            # add --start to launch `openshell dev --headless` on demand
```

Configure it as an MCP server in your client:

```bash
claude mcp add my-app -- openshell mcp --project /path/to/app       # Claude Code
```

```json
{ "mcpServers": { "my-app": { "command": "openshell", "args": ["mcp", "--project", "/path/to/app"] } } }
```

The stdio server forwards to the running shell and reconnects automatically, so the agent can be started before the
app. If the app is not running, `tools/list` still works and tool calls explain how to start it.

### MCP over HTTP

`POST {control_url}/mcp` (full profile) and `POST {control_url}/mcp/app` (app profile) implement the Streamable HTTP
transport (JSON responses). They require
`Authorization: Bearer <token>` from `.openshell/runtime.json`. Because the port and token change on each start,
stdio is more convenient; set `runtime.control_port` for a fixed port.

### From another device (remote gateway)

With `"runtime": { "remote": { "enabled": true } }` the app profile is also reachable from other devices – for
example an agent on a laptop using an app hosted on a phone. `openshell remote` prints the URL and a ready MCP client
configuration (`{ "url": "http://<ip>:7420/mcp/app", "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer <pairing token>" } }`).
Only the app's functions are exposed; see [platforms.md](platforms.md#remote-access).

### Plain HTTP / JSON

```
GET  /v1/tools                      list tools with permission and access (allowed / approval / denied)
POST /v1/tools/{name}               body = arguments → { "ok": true, "result": ... } or { "ok": false, "result": { "error": "..." } }
```

Send `X-OpenShell-Agent: <name>` to identify the agent in the audit log. From a terminal: `openshell call <tool> '<json>'`.

## Tools

| Tool | Scope | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `app_info` | read | Overview: app, mode, services, permissions, capabilities, hints. Call first. |
| `runtime_status` | read | State, pid, port, URL, restarts, last error per service |
| `logs_read` | read | Log lines (`service`, `since`, `limit`, `contains`, `errors_only`) |
| `capabilities_list` | read | Capabilities from config and frontend |
| `config_get` | read | Effective configuration |
| `providers_list` | read | Configured and detected AI providers with models |
| `audit_read` | read | Recent agent actions |
| `ui_pages` | ui | Pages connected to the UI bridge |
| `ui_snapshot` | ui | Title, URL, headings, dialogs, text and interactive elements with refs |
| `ui_click` | ui | Click by `ref`, `selector` or `text` |
| `ui_fill` | ui | Set input/textarea/select/checkbox/contenteditable (`label`, `value`, `submit`) |
| `ui_press` | ui | Key press (`Enter`, `Escape`, …) |
| `ui_read_text` | ui | Text of page or element |
| `ui_wait_for` | ui | Wait for selector/text (or its disappearance) |
| `ui_navigate` | ui | Navigate to `path` (SPA-friendly) or `url` |
| `ui_reload` | ui | Reload the frontend |
| `window_control` | ui | show / hide / focus / minimize / maximize / unmaximize |
| `notify` | ui | Native notification |
| `app_invoke` | capability's scope | Invoke a capability by name |
| `cap_<name>` | capability's scope | One tool per capability |
| `service_start` / `service_stop` / `service_restart` | services | Waits until the service is healthy and returns recent logs on failure |
| `fs_list` / `fs_read` / `fs_search` | files | Project files |
| `fs_write` | code | Create/overwrite a project file |
| `db_list` / `db_schema` / `db_query` | read | Databases, schema, read-only SQL (per database `agent_access` ≥ `read`) |
| `db_execute` | actions | SQL that changes data or schema (`agent_access: write`) |
| `task_run` | system | Run a task from `tasks` and return its output |
| `ui_eval` | system | Evaluate JavaScript in the page |

## Resources and notifications

Besides tools, the MCP server offers read-only **resources**: `openshell://status`, `openshell://config`,
`openshell://logs`, `openshell://capabilities` (developer profile), `openshell://app` (app profile) and
`openshell://db/<name>/schema` for every database agents may read.

`openshell mcp` (stdio) sends `notifications/tools/list_changed` whenever the tool list changes – for example when the
frontend registers an action, an OpenAPI document is imported or the app is started after the agent connected.

## UI automation

`ui_snapshot` returns a compact, semantic view of the page:

```json
{
  "url": "http://127.0.0.1:52471/",
  "title": "Todo App",
  "headings": [{ "level": 1, "text": "Todo App" }],
  "elements": [
    { "ref": "e1", "role": "textbox", "name": "New todo", "value": "" },
    { "ref": "e2", "role": "button", "name": "Add" },
    { "ref": "e6", "role": "checkbox", "name": "Buy milk", "checked": false }
  ],
  "text": "Todo App 3 todos · 1 done …",
  "actions": [{ "name": "set_filter", "description": "…" }]
}
```

Use the refs with `ui_click {"ref": "e2"}` or `ui_fill {"ref": "e1", "value": "…", "submit": true}`. Refs stay stable
while the element exists; take a new snapshot after larger UI changes. The bridge (`bridge.js`) is injected into the
desktop WebView and into pages served by OpenShell's static server, so it works with any framework and also in
browser mode (`openshell dev --headless`). Password values are never included in snapshots.

## Capabilities: the application's own functions

Prefer capabilities over UI automation – they are faster and more reliable, and they are what the app profile
exposes. Three sources:

- **OpenAPI import** – set `"openapi": "/openapi.json"` (FastAPI), `"/v3/api-docs"` (Spring/springdoc),
  `"/swagger/v1/swagger.json"` (ASP.NET) or a file/URL on a service. When the service becomes healthy, every operation
  becomes a tool: name from `operationId`, input schema from path/query parameters and the JSON request body,
  `GET` → scope `read`, other methods → `actions`. Filter with `{ "location": "...", "include": [...], "exclude": [...], "prefix": "shop" }`.
- **Declared** in `openshell.json` (`capabilities`), backed by an HTTP endpoint, a **script** (`run` – JSON in on
  stdin, JSON out on stdout, no server needed) or a task.
- **Databases**: with `agent_access` `read`/`write`, the app profile also offers `db_list`, `db_schema`, `db_query`
  and `db_execute` – an app can be *only* a database plus functions.
- **Registered by the frontend** at runtime with the SDK:

```js
OpenShell.agent.registerAction("set_filter", {
  description: "Show all, open or done todos",
  permission: "ui",
  input_schema: { type: "object", properties: { filter: { enum: ["all", "open", "done"] } } },
}, ({ filter }) => setFilter(filter));
```

## Permissions and approvals

Every tool needs exactly one scope:

| Scope | Allows | Default dev | Default prod |
|---|---|---|---|
| `read` | state, logs, config, capabilities list | ✅ | ✅ |
| `ui` | UI automation, window control, notifications | ✅ | ✅ |
| `actions` | capabilities that change data | ✅ | ✅ |
| `services` | start/stop/restart services | ✅ | – |
| `files` | read project files | ✅ | – |
| `code` | write project files | ✅ | – |
| `system` | declared tasks, JavaScript evaluation | – | – |

Configure with `agents.permissions`. Scopes in `agents.approval_required` (default `["system"]`) need a human
decision: the desktop app shows a dialog (and the runtime panel lists pending requests), headless mode prints the
request; answer with `openshell approve <id>` / `openshell deny <id>`. Unanswered requests are denied after
`approval_timeout_ms`.

Every call – allowed, denied, rejected or failed – is appended to `.openshell/audit.jsonl` with agent name, channel,
tool, scope, (truncated) arguments, outcome and duration. View it with `openshell audit`.

The runtime panel of the desktop app (title bar right-click → *Runtime panel* → *AI agents*) shows the effective
permissions: what each scope allows, development vs. production, which scopes ask for approval, and every agent
session and paired device with what it effectively may do. The same data: `openshell agents`, `GET /v1/agents`.

## Agent sessions

By default every agent connected through `openshell mcp` uses the admin token of `.openshell/runtime.json` and gets
the app's agent permissions. To tell agents apart and limit each one, give it its own session:

```bash
openshell agents token claude --scopes read,actions       # app profile: only the app's functions
openshell agents token builder --full                      # developer tools as well
openshell agents tokens                                    # list
openshell agents revoke claude                             # stops working at once, also while the app runs
```

The token (`osa_…`) is shown once and stored as a SHA-256 hash in `<data>/agent-sessions.json`. Use it with
`openshell mcp --token osa_…`, the environment variable `OPENSHELL_AGENT_TOKEN` (also for an installed app's
`--mcp`), or as `Authorization: Bearer` on the control API. A session

- gets at most what `agents.permissions` grants in the current mode, limited to its `--scopes`,
- with the app profile may only use `/mcp/app`; with `--full` also `/mcp` and `/v1/tools` – never the admin API,
- is written to the audit log as `session:<name>`.

`openshell agents token` prints a ready MCP client configuration:

```json
{ "mcpServers": { "claude": { "command": "openshell", "args": ["mcp", "--app", "--project", "/path/to/app"],
  "env": { "OPENSHELL_AGENT_TOKEN": "osa_…" } } } }
```

Paired devices on the remote gateway work the same way: `openshell remote pair laptop --scopes read` limits what
an agent on that device may do.

## Security

- The control API listens on `127.0.0.1` only and requires a bearer token. The admin token lives in
  `.openshell/runtime.json` (mode 0600 on Unix, ignored by git).
- Requests with a foreign `Host` header (DNS rebinding) or a non-allow-listed `Origin` (other websites) are rejected.
- The frontend gets a separate app token limited to `/v1/sdk/*` and the bridge, with `agents.sdk_permissions`.
- Application frontends loaded from http(s) URLs get no Tauri IPC access.
- File tools reject absolute paths, `..`, symlink escapes and OpenShell's state directory; `fs_write` also protects `.git`.
- Agents cannot run arbitrary shell commands; only tasks declared in the config, under the `system` scope.
- The remote gateway (off by default) exposes only the app profile, uses its own pairing token, rejects browser
  requests (`Origin`) and audits calls with the channel `remote`. Device tokens can carry their own scopes.
- Agent session tokens (`osa_…`) reach only the MCP endpoints and the tools API, never the admin API.
- With `agents.enabled: false` (the default) agents cannot connect at all.
- Limits: the permission layer governs cooperating agents. A local process running as the same user can read the token
  file; OpenShell is not a sandbox against local malware.

## A typical agent loop

1. `app_info` → understand the app, its services and capabilities.
2. Edit code with the agent's own file tools (or `fs_write`).
3. Services with `watch` restart automatically; otherwise `service_restart`. Check `runtime_status` / `logs_read {"errors_only": true}`.
4. `ui_reload` (static frontends reload automatically), then `ui_snapshot` and `ui_click` / `ui_fill` to verify the feature like a user would.

================================================================================

# Installers (`openshell package`)

`openshell package` turns an OpenShell project into a native installer – without writing or compiling any desktop
code for your app.

```bash
cargo build --release -p openshell-desktop   # once: the generic shell binary
openshell package                            # build + installer for the current platform
openshell package --target msi --out dist    # other formats, copy results to dist/
```

## What happens

1. `openshell build` runs (skip with `--skip-build`): compiled services (`services[].build`, e.g. Maven, CMake) and
   the frontend (`frontend.build`).
2. The application files are staged into `app/` (see *Which files are shipped*).
3. The generic `openshell-desktop` binary is copied, renamed to your app (`my-app.exe`) and **re-branded with your
   icon** (`app.icon`, PNG – OpenShell's icon if unset). No compiler is involved.
4. The Tauri bundler produces the installer(s):

| Platform | Formats (`--target` / `package.targets`) | Default |
|---|---|---|
| Windows | `nsis` (setup.exe, per-user install, no admin rights), `msi` | `nsis` |
| macOS | `app`, `dmg` | `app`, `dmg` |
| Linux | `deb`, `rpm`, `appimage` | `deb`, `appimage` |

The bundler downloads its tools (NSIS, WiX, appimagetool) on first use. The staging directory
`.openshell/package/bin/` is also a **portable build**: run `my-app.exe` there without installing.

## Installed app behaviour

```
%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\My App\        (Windows, NSIS per-user install)
  my-app.exe                           the shell, with your icon
  app\openshell.json                   your application
  app\...
```

- Starts in **production mode** (agent permissions from `agents.permissions.production`).
- State lives in a per-user directory named after the bundle identifier, e.g.
  `%LOCALAPPDATA%\com.example.myapp\` (Windows), `~/Library/Application Support/com.example.myapp/` (macOS),
  `~/.local/share/com.example.myapp/` (Linux): logs, audit log, `runtime.json` and **`data/`**, which services get as
  `OPENSHELL_DATA_DIR`. Store your database/files there so they survive updates and uninstalls.
- Single instance: starting the app again focuses the running window. A background instance started for an agent
  (`--mcp`) is replaced by the window.
- `my-app.exe --mcp` is an MCP server for AI agents on the user's machine (see [agents.md](agents.md#using-an-installed-app)).
- `my-app.exe --headless` runs the services without a window.

## Configuration

```json
{
  "app": { "name": "My App", "id": "com.example.myapp", "version": "1.2.0", "icon": "assets/icon.png" },
  "package": {
    "publisher": "Example Inc.",
    "homepage": "https://example.com",
    "copyright": "© 2026 Example Inc.",
    "license_file": "LICENSE",
    "targets": ["nsis", "msi"],
    "exclude": ["docs", "**/*.test.js"],
    "include": []
  }
}
```

`app.version` must be a semantic version (`1.2.0`). `package.identifier` overrides `app.id`.

### Which files are shipped

By default the whole project **except** `.git`, `.openshell`, `node_modules`, `__pycache__`, `*.pyc`, virtualenvs,
`.gradle`, IDE folders. Add `exclude` patterns (globs, relative to the project), or list exactly what to ship with
`include` (the config file is always included):

```json
"package": { "include": ["openshell.json", "web", "backend/build/bin"] }   // C++: only the compiled binary
"package": { "exclude": ["backend/src"] }                                 // Java: ship classes, not sources
"package": { "exclude": ["frontend/src", "frontend/public"] }             // ship only frontend/dist
```

## Runtimes

The installer contains the shell and your app files. Interpreters and runtimes your services need – Python, Node.js,
a JRE – must exist on the target machine, **or you ship them with the app**:

```bash
openshell runtime add python 3.12      # declares it in openshell.json and downloads it into runtimes/python
openshell runtime add node 22
openshell runtime add java 21          # Temurin JRE
openshell package                      # the runtime folder is part of the installer
```

Bundled runtimes come first in `PATH` for every service, setup and build step, function and task, so `python
main.py` uses them without any change. They are built for one system: the release workflow runs
`openshell runtime install` on each build machine before `openshell package`. See
[configuration.md](configuration.md#runtimes). Compiled services (C++, Rust, Go, GraalVM native images, self-contained
.NET) need nothing extra. Declare the versions a service needs with `requires` (`{ "python": ">=3.10" }`);
`openshell doctor` checks them and the app logs a warning at start when they are not met. If a runtime is missing,
the loading screen shows the error (`java was not found in PATH`).

## Portable app bundle (`.osapp`)

```bash
openshell package --target bundle        # dist/my-app-1.2.0.osapp – works on every platform, also in Termux
```

A bundle is a zip with the shipped files (same `include` / `exclude` rules) and
`openshell-bundle.json` (app, identifier, version). It runs **unchanged** on every OpenShell host:

| Host | How |
|---|---|
| Android app | open or share the `.osapp` with OpenShell ([android-app.md](android-app.md)) |
| Termux, servers, desktops with the CLI | `openshell install my-app-1.2.0.osapp --start` |

`openshell install` unpacks into `~/.openshell/apps/<identifier>/` (`OPENSHELL_APPS_DIR`); installing
a newer bundle replaces the files and keeps the app's data (`.openshell/`). `openshell apps` lists
installed bundles.

## One link per system

A developer builds once, users download one file for their system – without changing the program.

```bash
openshell release workflow               # writes .github/workflows/openshell-release.yml
git tag v1.2.0 && git push origin v1.2.0
```

On every tag the workflow builds in parallel and publishes a GitHub release with:

| File | For |
|---|---|
| `My App_1.2.0_x64-setup.exe` | Windows (NSIS, per-user install) |
| `My App_1.2.0_aarch64.dmg`, `My App_1.2.0_x64.dmg` | macOS Apple Silicon / Intel |
| `my-app_1.2.0_amd64.AppImage`, `.deb` | Linux |
| `my-app-1.2.0.osapp` | Android (OpenShell app, Termux), servers, any host |
| `downloads.json` | machine-readable list: platform, arch, URL, size, SHA-256 |
| `index.html` | download page that offers the visitor's system first |

`https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/releases/latest` always points at the newest release. Without
GitHub, build on each system and run `openshell release manifest dist --base-url https://example.com/my-app/v1.2.0`
to get the same `downloads.json` and page for any web server.

## Update checks

```json
"package": { "update_url": "https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/releases/latest/download/downloads.json" }
```

`openshell update` and the control API (`GET /v1/update`) compare the running version with the
newest release and return the right download for the current system. Installing updates
automatically (download, verify, replace) is planned.

## Signing

Unsigned installers trigger SmartScreen / Gatekeeper warnings. Configure signing in
`openshell.json`; secrets stay in the environment or the certificate store:

```json
"package": {
  "signing": {
    "windows": { "certificate_thumbprint": "A1B2…", "timestamp_url": "http://timestamp.digicert.com" },
    "macos": { "signing_identity": "Developer ID Application: Example Inc. (TEAMID)" }
  }
}
```

| Platform | Setting | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Windows | `certificate_thumbprint` | Certificate in the user's/machine's store (import a `.pfx` first); SHA-256 digest |
| Windows | `sign_command` | Any signer, e.g. Azure Trusted Signing or a cloud HSM: `["trusted-signing-cli", "-e", "…", "%1"]` (`%1` = file) |
| Windows | `timestamp_url` | RFC 3161 timestamp server, keeps signatures valid after the certificate expires |
| macOS | `signing_identity` | `Developer ID Application: …` (hardened runtime on), `-` for ad-hoc |
| macOS | `entitlements`, `provider_short_name` | Optional |
| macOS | notarisation | `APPLE_ID`, `APPLE_PASSWORD`, `APPLE_TEAM_ID` (or `APPLE_API_KEY`, `APPLE_API_ISSUER`) in the environment |

The release workflow imports certificates from repository secrets (`WINDOWS_CERTIFICATE`,
`APPLE_CERTIFICATE`, …, see the comments at its top). Certificates and Apple Developer accounts are
not part of OpenShell – you need your own.


================================================================================
FILE: docs/platforms.md
================================================================================

# Platforms: desktop, server and Android

OpenShell is not tied to the desktop. The runtime, the agent layer, the control API and the
configuration are the same everywhere; a small **platform adapter** decides how programs are
started and how the app lifecycle is handled. This page describes the platform model, what works
on Android today and where the Android work is going.

## Goals

- **One core, several platforms.** `openshell-core` runs unchanged on Windows, macOS, Linux,
  headless servers and Android. Platform code lives in adapters and hosts, not in the core.
- **The phone as a personal runtime and mini server.** Apps, services, databases, automations
  and agents generated by AI run locally on the phone and stay reachable for your other devices.
- **AI builds, the user does not edit code.** Agents create, extend, test and manage apps through
  the same MCP tools as on the desktop; the platform tells them which building blocks exist there.
- **Connected devices.** Desktop, phone and server are meant to manage and develop projects
  together (see [device mesh](#device-mesh-in-progress)).

## Layers

```
            ┌───────────────────────── hosts ─────────────────────────┐
            │ desktop app (Tauri)   headless CLI   Android app (Kotlin) │
            │ window, tray, dialogs  terminal       Activity + WebView, │
            │                                       foreground service  │
            └──────────────┬──────────────────────────────┬──────────────┘
                           │ Host trait                    │ lifecycle events
            ┌──────────────▼──────────────────────────────▼──────────────┐
            │ openshell-core: Shell, control API, MCP, remote gateway    │
            │ openshell-agent: policy, approvals, audit, UI bridge       │
            │ openshell-runtime: plan, supervisor, health, logs, static  │
            │                    server, databases, lifecycle            │
            └──────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                           │ RuntimeAdapter
            ┌──────────────▼─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
            │ DesktopAdapter (desktop, server)   AndroidAdapter (app)     │
            │ any program in PATH, job objects   system tools + programs  │
            │ / process groups                   bundled with the app     │
            │                                    TermuxAdapter (Termux)   │
            │                                    pkg-installed toolchains │
            └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

| Piece | Where | Responsibility |
|---|---|---|
| `Platform` | `crates/config` | `desktop`, `android`, `server` – used in `services[].platforms` |
| `RuntimeAdapter` | `crates/runtime/src/platform.rs` | builds every command (services, setup, build, functions, tasks), reports `Capabilities` |
| `DesktopAdapter` | same | any program from `PATH` or the project; `server` variant without window and tray |
| `AndroidAdapter` | same | the Android app: only system tools (`/system/bin`) and programs registered by the host (`node` → `libnode.so`) |
| `TermuxAdapter` | same | Android in Termux: everything installed with `pkg install` (Python, Node.js, Java, Rust, Go, databases) |
| `LifecycleEvent` | `crates/runtime/src/lib.rs` | `foreground`, `background`, `low_memory`, `power_save`, `network` |
| `Host` | `crates/core/src/lib.rs` | window, notifications, approvals – implemented per front-end |
| Remote gateway | `crates/core/src/remote*` | the app profile and exposed services for other devices: tokens, allowlist, rate limit, TLS |
| Android host | `apps/android`, `crates/android` | Kotlin app + JNI bridge – see [android-app.md](android-app.md) |

`Runtime::new` / `Shell::launch` pick the adapter for the platform the binary was built for.
Hosts can pass their own with `Runtime::with_adapter` / `Shell::launch_with`.

## Capabilities

Every runtime reports what its platform offers. Agents see it in `app_info` and `GET /v1/status`:

```json
"platform": {
  "platform": "android", "os": "android", "arch": "aarch64",
  "processes": "restricted", "background": "foreground_service",
  "file_watching": true, "app_window": true, "tray": false, "installers": false,
  "toolchains": false, "wake_lock": true
}
```

| Field | Desktop | Server | Android app | Termux |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `processes` | `full` | `full` | `restricted` – system tools and bundled programs | `full` |
| `background` | `always` | `always` | `foreground_service` | `foreground_service` (wake lock) |
| `app_window` / `tray` | yes / yes | no / no | yes / no | no / no (browser) |
| `installers` | yes | no | no | no (`.osapp` bundles yes) |
| `toolchains` – build steps, dev servers, `npm`/`pip`/`cargo` | yes | yes | no | yes |
| `wake_lock` | no | no | yes | yes |

## Configuration

```json
{
  "services": [
    { "name": "compiler", "command": "cargo run", "platforms": ["desktop", "server"] },
    { "name": "sync", "command": ["node", "sync.mjs"], "background": "pause" }
  ],
  "runtime": { "remote": { "enabled": true, "bind": "0.0.0.0", "port": 7420 } }
}
```

- `services[].platforms` – only run on these platforms. Like `modes`, services for other platforms
  are left out of the plan and dependencies on them are dropped.
- `services[].background` – `keep` (default) or `pause`: stop while the app is in the background,
  start again when it returns. Only matters on platforms with `background: foreground_service`.
- `runtime.remote` – the [remote gateway](#remote-access).

## Android

### What runs on Android

Android allows an app to execute only files inside its APK (the native library directory) and
system tools – files written at runtime cannot be executed (W^X, Android 10+). There is no `PATH`
with toolchains. The `AndroidAdapter` follows these rules and turns violations into a clear error
that tells the developer or the agent what to use instead:

```
`cargo` cannot run on Android: apps may only start system tools and programs shipped with the
app (bundled: node). Use a static frontend, the built-in database or functions for a bundled
interpreter, or limit this service with "platforms": ["desktop", "server"]
```

| Building block | On Android |
|---|---|
| Static frontend (`frontend.dist`) | ✅ built-in static server |
| Built-in database (SQLite, migrations, SDK, agents) | ✅ compiled into OpenShell |
| Functions (`capabilities[].run`) | ✅ with system tools (`sh`) or a bundled interpreter |
| Services | ✅ with a bundled program (`node`, `python`, own binaries in the APK) |
| HTTP capabilities, OpenAPI import, UI bridge, MCP | ✅ unchanged |
| Dev-server frontends, build steps with toolchains | ❌ – build on the desktop, or limit with `platforms` |

The host registers what it bundles:

```rust
let adapter = AndroidAdapter::new()                        // allows /system/bin
    .with_executable_dir(native_library_dir)               // every executable in the APK
    .with_program("node", native_library_dir.join("libnode.so"))
    .with_program("python", native_library_dir.join("libpython.so"));
let shell = Shell::launch_with(project, Mode::Production, host, Arc::new(adapter)).await?;
```

Without a host the adapter reads `OPENSHELL_ANDROID_EXEC_DIRS` (`:`-separated) and
`OPENSHELL_ANDROID_PROGRAMS` (`node=/path/libnode.so;python=/path/libpython.so`). Inside Termux
the [`TermuxAdapter`](#termux-apps-on-the-phone) is used instead.

### Termux: apps on the phone

[Termux](https://termux.dev) is a Linux environment for Android with its own package manager. The
OpenShell CLI runs there and detects it (`$PREFIX` / `$TERMUX_VERSION`), so the phone becomes a
development machine and a portable host – no computer needed:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RobinsSuperSchmiede/EDA/main/scripts/install.sh | sh
pkg install python nodejs openjdk-17 rust golang postgresql   # what your apps need
openshell create notes --with frontend,backend,database
cd notes && openshell dev          # dev server, file watching, agents – like on the desktop
openshell start --headless         # production; open the URL in the phone's browser
openshell package --target bundle  # notes-0.1.0.osapp for the Android app or other hosts
```

- Every program from `$PREFIX/bin` runs: services, setup and build steps (`npm install`, `pip`,
  `cargo build`, `mvn`), dev servers and functions. `python` falls back to `python3`.
- `openshell doctor` shows the platform and turns missing programs into `pkg install …` hints.
- While an app runs, OpenShell holds a Termux wake lock (`termux-wake-lock`, from the Termux:API
  package) so services keep running with the screen off, and releases it on stop.
- Databases: the built-in SQLite needs nothing; PostgreSQL, Redis or MariaDB from `pkg` run as
  services and can be [exposed](remote-access.md) to other devices.
- `OPENSHELL_ANDROID_MODE=app` forces the restricted app adapter (to test what the Android app
  allows); `OPENSHELL_ANDROID_MODE=termux` forces the Termux adapter in Termux-like environments.

### Lifecycle, battery and network

Android stops apps in the background. The host forwards the Activity and system events:

| Android | `LifecycleEvent` | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `onStart` | `foreground` | paused services start again |
| `onStop` | `background` | services with `"background": "pause"` stop |
| `onTrimMemory(RUNNING_CRITICAL)` | `low_memory` | pausable services stop |
| `PowerManager.isPowerSaveMode` | `power_save` | reported to agents and hosts |
| `ConnectivityManager` callback | `network` | reported (`connected`, `metered`) |

`Runtime::keep_alive()` lists the active services that must keep running (`background: keep`).
While it is not empty the Android host keeps a **foreground service** (type `specialUse` or
`dataSync`, with a persistent notification) alive and asks the user once to exempt the app from
battery optimisation, so the phone can act as an always-on server. When the list becomes empty
the host stops the foreground service and Android may suspend the app.

Hosts send events with `Shell::lifecycle(event)`; for testing on any platform use the CLI or API:

```bash
openshell lifecycle background     # services with "background": "pause" stop
openshell lifecycle foreground     # … and start again
curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "content-type: application/json" -d '{"kind":"low_memory"}' $URL/v1/lifecycle
```

### Status

- ✅ The core and the CLI build for `aarch64-linux-android` and `x86_64-linux-android` (CI checks
  the Android build on every push).
- ✅ Verified on an Android 16 emulator: `openshell dev --headless` serves a static frontend,
  migrates the database, runs functions through `/system/bin/sh`, leaves desktop-only services
  out, pauses and resumes services on lifecycle events and serves the app profile to a laptop
  through the remote gateway.
- ✅ Termux: `TermuxAdapter` with toolchains, wake lock and `pkg install` hints; prebuilt CLI for
  `aarch64-linux-android` in releases, `install.sh` detects Termux.
- 🚧 Android app: Kotlin host + JNI bridge in `apps/android` / `crates/android`, AAB build for the
  Play Store in CI – see [android-app.md](android-app.md).

### The Android app

The OpenShell Android app is a host around the unchanged core – see [android-app.md](android-app.md):

1. **Shell app** – Kotlin Activity with a WebView (no JavaScript bridge for app pages) and the core
   as a JNI library (`libopenshell_android.so`).
2. **Foreground service** (`specialUse`) – keeps the runtime alive, shows a notification with the
   running services, forwards lifecycle, memory and network events, partial wake lock.
3. **App manager** – install apps from `.osapp` bundles (file picker, share sheet), open, stop.
4. **Bundled runtimes** (planned) – Node.js and Python as `lib*.so` in the APK, registered
   automatically when present.
5. **On-device agents** – remote agents through the gateway today; local models planned.

## Remote access

The remote gateway makes an app usable from other devices – a laptop agent using functions of an
app hosted on the phone, a browser opening a website the phone serves, a desktop tool using a
database on the phone. Off by default; tokens per device, an address allowlist, rate limits with
lockout, TLS, opt-in exposure per service and an audit trail can be combined:

```json
"runtime": { "remote": { "enabled": true, "allow": ["192.168.1.0/24"], "tls": { "enabled": true },
                         "expose": [{ "service": "frontend", "port": 8080 }] } }
```

```bash
openshell remote pair laptop     # token for one device, QR code, links
openshell remote                 # URLs, fingerprint, devices, blocked addresses
```

Full guide: [remote-access.md](remote-access.md).

## Device mesh (in progress)

Desktop, phone and server running OpenShell should form one personal mesh:

- ✅ **Pairing** – per-device tokens with a QR code / pairing URI (`openshell remote pair`), TLS with
  pinned self-signed certificates, revocation per device.
- **Discovery** – mDNS (`_openshell._tcp`) in the local network, VPN addresses otherwise.
- **Remote control API** – manage services, logs and approvals of another device's apps with the
  same CLI (`openshell --device phone status`).
- **Project sync** – projects as folders synchronised between devices (git-based), so an agent can
  develop on the desktop and deploy to the phone (`openshell deploy --device phone`).
- **Placement** – `services[].platforms` already lets one project describe what runs where; the
  mesh adds "run this service on the server, the UI on the phone".


================================================================================
FILE: docs/cli.md
================================================================================

# CLI reference

Global option: `-p, --project <dir>` – project directory (default: current directory or the nearest parent with an
`openshell.json`). Environment: `OPENSHELL_LOG` (log filter, e.g. `debug`), `OPENSHELL_DESKTOP` (path of the desktop
binary), `NO_COLOR`, `OPENSHELL_APPS_DIR` (installed bundles), `OPENSHELL_ANDROID_MODE` (`termux` / `app`, see
[platforms.md](platforms.md#termux-apps-on-the-phone)).

## Project setup

| Command | Description |
|---|---|
| `openshell create <name> [-t <template>]` | New project from a template (`vanilla-python` default, `react-python`, `react-node`, `vue-python`, `svelte-go`, `vanilla-java`, `vanilla-cpp`, `custom`). `--list` shows all. |
| `openshell create <name> --with frontend,backend,database,functions [--lang python\|node]` | New project composed of [building blocks](building-blocks.md). Without `--template`/`--with` the terminal asks. |
| `openshell add frontend \| backend [--lang …] \| database [name] \| function <name> [--lang …]` | Add a building block to the current app (files + `openshell.json`). |
| `openshell init [--name <n>] [--toml] [--force]` | Generate a config for an existing project (auto-detection) and an `AGENTS.md` for coding agents if none exists. |
| `openshell doctor` | Validate config, commands, directories, ports, desktop binary, WebView2, toolchain. Exit code 1 on errors. |
| `openshell schema` | Print the JSON Schema of the configuration. |
| `openshell guide` | Print the guide for AI coding agents that build apps on OpenShell (docs/ai/app-development.md). |
| `openshell build` | Production build: `services[].build` (C++, Java, …) and `frontend.build` (with `frontend.setup` if needed). |
| `openshell package [-t nsis\|msi\|dmg\|deb\|…\|bundle] [-o dir] [--skip-build]` | Build a native installer, or with `-t bundle` the portable app bundle (`.osapp`, also on Android/Termux) – see [installers.md](installers.md). |
| `openshell release workflow [--force]` | Write `.github/workflows/openshell-release.yml`: a tag push builds Windows, macOS, Linux installers and the `.osapp` bundle and publishes them with a download page. |
| `openshell release manifest [dir] [--base-url <url>]` | Write `downloads.json` (platform, file, size, SHA-256) and a download page (`index.html`) for the files in `dir` (default `dist`). |
| `openshell install <file.osapp> [--start]` | Install an app bundle into `~/.openshell/apps/<identifier>` (`OPENSHELL_APPS_DIR`); app data survives updates. |
| `openshell apps` | List installed app bundles. |
| `openshell update` | Check `package.update_url` for a newer release and print the download for this system. |
| `openshell runtime` | Bundled runtimes: declared, installed version, `requires` checks. |
| `openshell runtime add <python\|node\|java> [version] [--path dir] [--no-install]` | Declare a runtime in `runtimes` and download it into the project (see [configuration.md](configuration.md#runtimes)). |
| `openshell runtime install [name] [--force]` | Download the declared runtimes for this system (checksums verified; installed ones are skipped). |
| `openshell runtime remove <name> [--keep-files]` | Remove a runtime from `runtimes` and delete its folder. |
| `openshell languages` | Backend languages: support level (tested, less tested, by contract), runtime they need, templates. |

## Running

| Command | Description |
|---|---|
| `openshell dev [--headless]` | Development mode. Opens the desktop window (or runs headless for the browser) and streams logs. Ctrl+C stops everything. |
| `openshell start [--headless] [--detach]` | Production mode. `--detach` returns immediately and keeps the app running in the background. |
| `openshell stop` | Stop the whole shell (all services, window). |
| `openshell stop <service>` | Stop one service. |
| `openshell run <service>` | Start a stopped service (and its dependencies). |
| `openshell restart <service>` | Restart a service and wait until it is healthy. |

## Inspecting

| Command | Description |
|---|---|
| `openshell status [--json]` | Mode, URLs, services (state, pid, port, CPU, memory, restarts, errors), bridged pages, pending approvals. |
| `openshell logs [service] [-f] [-n 100] [--errors] [--grep <text>]` | Logs of all or one service. |
| `openshell audit [-n 30]` | Recent agent actions. |
| `openshell remote` | Remote gateway: URLs, MCP endpoint, TLS fingerprint, allowlist, exposed services, paired devices, blocked addresses, shared token and an MCP client configuration (`runtime.remote`). |
| `openshell remote pair <device> [--no-qr] [--scopes read,actions]` | Create a token for one device (shown once) with a QR code / pairing URI and links to exposed services. `--scopes` limits what the device may do. |
| `openshell remote devices` | Paired devices with last use. |
| `openshell remote revoke <device>` | Revoke one device's token. |
| `openshell remote unblock <address>` | Lift the block of an address after too many failed logins. |
| `openshell lifecycle <foreground\|background\|low-memory>` | Simulate a mobile lifecycle event, e.g. to test `"background": "pause"`. |

## Agents

| Command | Description |
|---|---|
| `openshell mcp [--app] [--start] [--token osa_…]` | MCP server over stdio. `--app`: only the application's own functions (agents that *use* the app). `--start`: start the app headless if it is not running. `--token` (or `OPENSHELL_AGENT_TOKEN`): use an agent session's token and scopes instead of the admin token. |
| `openshell agents` | Agent layer on/off, effective permissions per mode, agent sessions and paired devices. |
| `openshell agents enable` / `disable` | Set `agents.enabled` in openshell.json (agents are opt-in). |
| `openshell agents token <name> [--scopes read,actions] [--full]` | Create an agent session with its own token (shown once) and scopes; prints an MCP client configuration. `--full`: developer tools too. |
| `openshell agents tokens` / `revoke <name>` | List agent sessions / revoke one (takes effect at once, also while the app runs). |
| `openshell tools [--json]` | Tools with scope and current access (allowed / approval / denied). |
| `openshell call <tool> ['<json args>']` | Call a tool as agent `cli`, e.g. `openshell call ui_click '{"text":"Save"}'`. |
| `openshell approvals` | Pending approval requests. |
| `openshell approve <id>` / `openshell deny <id>` | Answer an approval request. |


================================================================================
FILE: docs/sdk.md
================================================================================

# Frontend SDK (`@openshell/sdk`)

The SDK is optional. Your frontend works unchanged inside and outside OpenShell; the SDK adds access to the runtime,
the native window and the agent layer when available.

## Loading

The shell serves the SDK at `{control_url}/sdk.js`, so no package installation is needed:

```js
async function openshell() {
  if (!window.__OPENSHELL__) return null; // plain browser
  const { OpenShell } = await import(/* @vite-ignore */ `${window.__OPENSHELL__.api}/sdk.js`);
  return OpenShell;
}
```

Or copy `packages/sdk` into your project / install it from the repository (`npm install <path>/packages/sdk`) and
`import { OpenShell } from "@openshell/sdk"`.

## API

```ts
OpenShell.available: boolean            // running inside OpenShell?
OpenShell.mode: "development" | "production" | null
OpenShell.host: "desktop" | "browser" | null

await OpenShell.info()                  // app, mode, host, granted SDK permissions, service names

await OpenShell.runtime.status()        // read
await OpenShell.runtime.logs({ service: "backend", limit: 50 })   // read
await OpenShell.runtime.restart("backend")                         // services
await OpenShell.runtime.start("worker") / .stop("worker")          // services

await OpenShell.window.minimize() / maximize() / unmaximize() / show() / hide() / focus()   // ui
await OpenShell.notify("Export finished", "Saved to reports/q3.pdf")                       // ui
await OpenShell.providers()             // read – configured and local AI providers

// built-in databases (databases in openshell.json) – a frontend-only app can store data without a backend
await OpenShell.db.list()                                            // read
await OpenShell.db.query("SELECT * FROM notes WHERE done = ?", [0])  // read  → { columns, rows, row_count }
await OpenShell.db.execute("INSERT INTO notes (title) VALUES (:t)", { t: "Hi" })   // actions → { changes, last_insert_rowid }
await OpenShell.db.schema("notes")                                   // read

// the app's functions (capabilities) – the same ones agents use
await OpenShell.invoke("summarize_notes", { limit: 10 })            // the capability's own scope

const unregister = OpenShell.agent.registerAction(name, { description, input_schema, permission }, handler)
OpenShell.agent.unregisterAction(name)

await OpenShell.call(tool, args)        // any tool allowed by agents.sdk_permissions
```

Calls are checked against `agents.sdk_permissions` (default `["read", "ui"]`). To let the frontend write to a
database or call `actions` functions, add `"actions"` (`openshell add database` does this when the app has a
frontend); to restart services, add `"services"`. A database's `agent_access` limits agents only, not the app's own
frontend. Failures throw `OpenShellError`.

## Exposing frontend actions to agents

```js
OpenShell.agent.registerAction(
  "open_invoice",
  {
    description: "Open the invoice editor for an invoice id",
    permission: "ui",
    input_schema: { type: "object", properties: { id: { type: "string" } }, required: ["id"] },
  },
  async ({ id }) => {
    router.push(`/invoices/${id}`);
    return { opened: id };
  },
);
```

Agents discover it with `capabilities_list` and call it as `cap_open_invoice` or `app_invoke`. The handler runs in the
page; its return value (JSON) is sent back to the agent.

## Own title bar

With `"window": { "title_bar": "overlay" }` the desktop window has no system title bar (Windows, Linux) or shows
only the window buttons over the content (macOS), and the frontend draws its own. The desktop window provides:

```js
const win = window.__OPENSHELL__?.window;     // undefined in a plain browser
if (win?.title_bar === "overlay") {
  win.os;                 // "windows" | "macos" | "linux" – macOS: leave ~80px on the left for its buttons
  await win.minimize();
  await win.toggleMaximize();
  await win.close();      // respects close_to_tray
  await win.isMaximized();
  await win.showMenu();   // the runtime menu (services, logs, reload) at the cursor
}
```

Mark the bar with `data-tauri-drag-region="deep"`: dragging it moves the window, a double click maximizes it; buttons,
links and inputs inside keep working. These functions are allowed only for the app's frontend origin.


================================================================================
FILE: docs/control-api.md
================================================================================

# Control API

Every running shell exposes a local HTTP API on `127.0.0.1:<port>`. Its URL and admin token are written to
`<project>/.openshell/runtime.json` while the shell runs:

```json
{ "pid": 648, "url": "http://127.0.0.1:52472", "token": "…", "mode": "development", "host": "desktop", "app": "Todo App", "started_at": "…", "version": "0.1.0" }
```

Authenticate with `Authorization: Bearer <token>` (WebSocket: `?token=`). Requests with a foreign `Host` header or a
non-allow-listed `Origin` are rejected with 403.

Three kinds of token: the **admin** token of `runtime.json`, the **app** token the frontend gets (SDK and UI bridge
only), and **agent session** tokens (`osa_…`, `openshell agents token`) which reach `/mcp/app` – and with the full
profile `/mcp` and `/v1/tools` – with the session's scopes. With `agents.enabled: false` (the default) `/mcp`,
`/mcp/app`, `/v1/tools` and `/v1/ui/bridge` answer 403 for every token.

## Endpoints

| Method & path | Token | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `GET /v1/health` | – | `{ ok, app, mode, host, platform, version }` |
| `GET /sdk.js`, `GET /bridge.js` | – | Frontend SDK, UI bridge script |
| `GET /v1/status` (alias `/v1/info`) | admin | App, mode, host, platform capabilities, pid, URLs, services, bridged pages, pending approvals, agent permissions, `in_background`, `keep_alive`, `remote` |
| `POST /v1/services/{name}/{start\|stop\|restart}` | admin | Change the desired state (returns immediately) |
| `GET /v1/logs?service=&since=&limit=&contains=&errors_only=` | admin | `{ lines: [{ seq, ts, service, stream, text }], last_seq }` |
| `POST /v1/shutdown` | admin | Stop all services and exit |
| `GET /v1/approvals` | admin | `{ pending: [{ id, agent, tool, permission, summary, args, created_at, expires_at }] }` |
| `POST /v1/approvals/{id}/{approve\|deny}` | admin | Answer an approval request |
| `GET /v1/audit?limit=` | admin | Recent audit entries |
| `GET /v1/tools` | admin, session (full) | Tools with `permission`, `access` and `input_schema` (access for the caller) |
| `POST /v1/tools/{name}` | admin, session (full) | Call a tool with the **agent** policy (limited to a session's scopes). Header `X-OpenShell-Agent` names the agent. |
| `POST /mcp` | admin, session (full) | MCP Streamable HTTP (JSON-RPC, JSON responses, `Mcp-Session-Id`) |
| `POST /mcp/app` | admin, session | MCP with the app profile (the app's own functions) |
| `GET /v1/agents` | admin | Effective agent permissions: `enabled`, `granted`, `by_mode`, `approval_required`, `sdk_permissions`, `sessions` and `devices` with their effective scopes |
| `GET /v1/ui/bridge` | app or admin | WebSocket for `bridge.js` |
| `GET /v1/sdk/info` | app | App info and SDK permissions |
| `POST /v1/sdk/call/{tool}` | app | Call a tool with the **SDK** policy |
| `POST /v1/lifecycle` | admin | App lifecycle from the host: `{ "kind": "foreground" \| "background" \| "low_memory" }`, `{ "kind": "power_save", "enabled": true }`, `{ "kind": "network", "connected": true, "metered": false }` → paused/resumed services and `keep_alive` |
| `GET /v1/remote` | admin | Remote gateway: `enabled`, `urls`, `mcp_url`, shared `token` (if `shared_token`), `tls_fingerprint`, `allow`, `exposed`, `devices`, `blocked`, `pairing_uri` |
| `GET /v1/remote/devices` | admin | Paired devices (`name`, `paired_at`, `last_seen`, `scopes`) |
| `POST /v1/remote/devices` | admin | Pair a device: `{"name":"laptop","scopes":["read"]}` → its `token` (only in this answer) and `pairing_uri` |
| `POST /v1/remote/devices/{name}/revoke` | admin | Revoke a device's token |
| `POST /v1/remote/unblock` | admin | `{"address":"192.168.1.7"}` – lift a lockout |
| `GET /v1/update` | admin | `{configured, update: {current, latest, available, download, page}}` from `package.update_url` |

The optional remote gateway (`runtime.remote`) is a separate listener with `GET /v1/health`, `GET /v1/remote/info`
and `POST /mcp/app` only, authorised with the shared or a device token – see [remote-access.md](remote-access.md).

## Example

```bash
URL=$(jq -r .url .openshell/runtime.json); TOKEN=$(jq -r .token .openshell/runtime.json)
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" $URL/v1/status
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "X-OpenShell-Agent: my-script" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
     -d '{"service":"backend","errors_only":true}' $URL/v1/tools/logs_read
```
